idiom_name: EF Core MessageRecord entity over Microsoft.Data.Sqlite + Channel writer
implementation_notes: The store is an ordinary mapped table: a MessageRecord entity keyed by the message id plus a DbContext over Microsoft.Data.Sqlite (or any provider), so append is Add + SaveChangesAsync and reporting is a LINQ query - the classic Store and record split collapses into one entity plus a query surface, with the provider doing transactions and the engine doing durability. Because EF Core writes synchronously with the caller, the tap belongs off the request path: publish the record into a System.Threading.Channels.Channel<MessageRecord> (or a hosted BackgroundService) and let one consumer write batches, so a slow store degrades the audit trail instead of the API. Retention is a set-based sweep (ExecuteDeleteAsync with a timestamp filter, or partitioned tables where the database supports them), and the payload column carries the already-redacted projection. Hand-write the ADO.NET SqliteCommand form only where the mapping cost is measurable; the entity form stays right whenever the store is queried as data rather than as bytes.
pitfalls: SaveChanges on the request path makes an audit feature a latency and availability dependency of the API; write to a bounded Channel and batch in a background service, and document the drop policy when the channel is full.

SQLite serialises writers: a single SqliteConnection shared by concurrent requests throws 'database is locked' unless WAL is enabled and writes are funnelled through one writer, which is also what the Channel consumer gives you.
The audit table inherits your migrations: a payload contract change becomes a migration on stored history, so version the payload column and keep record changes additive.
The SQLite provider stores DateTimeOffset as text; comparing mixed offsets orders incorrectly, so normalise to UTC before writing and before filtering retention.
